messages:
Maddie: Thinking about per-org rate limits—we've been leaning on RPM + concurrency caps, but TPM (tokens/min) keeps coming up for cost-sensitive workloads. thoughts?
Jay: TPM makes a lot of sense for text-heavy customers (long generations). RPM undercounts cost.
Priya: Agreed. For short-chatty calls RPM is OK. Maybe hybrid: RPM for request shape X, TPM for generation-heavy.
Alex: Hybrid adds complexity to enforcement layer though. Our limiter currently keys on requests/sec buckets.
Maddie: Right. Implementation tradeoffs: do we add a parallel token-meter that charges as tokens stream, or estimate cost pre-accept?
Sam: Streaming token-metering is doable: increment on token emit, but needs strong idempotency for retries. ops impact likely higher.
Priya: What about concurrency caps (per-org) + a rolling token window (e.g., tokens per 60s)? Concurrency keeps latency SLOs, token window controls spend.
Jay: That seems pragmatic. Concurrency for headroom protection, token window for spend. Need a clear burst policy: allow short bursts up to N requests but drain token pool.
Maddie: UX question for console: show both metrics and expose a single knob for "cost profile" (conservative/standard/aggressive) that maps to these settings?
Alex: Nice — defaults could be: conservative -> low concurrency, strict TPM; standard -> moderate; aggressive -> higher concurrency + looser TPM.
Sam: For rollout, canary 1% orgs, monitor errors, token breaches, and latency. If we observe a rise in rejections at 1% -> rollback.
Priya: Metrics to track: token consumption rate, rejected requests by reason (concurrency vs tokens), tail latency, retry loops per org. Also alert on >3% of requests getting "rate_limit.exceeded" per org per hour.
Maddie: Policy config sketch (pseudo):
```yaml
policies:
  - org: default
    concurrency: 10
    token_window_seconds: 60
    token_limit: 100000
    burst_buffer_requests: 5
    burst_window_seconds: 10
```
Jay: Need to decide enforcement ordering: should concurrency be checked first (cheap), then token window (more stateful)? I vote concurrency first.
Alex: Concurrency-first also avoids spinning up token checks for obviously blocked requests.
Sam: Also add a soft-limit path: when token pool low, redirect to cheaper model variant automatically (routing policy). Should be a pluggable fallback.
Priya: Fallback routing will need precedence rules and instrumentation to ensure quality doesn't regress. tie into Optimize signals.
Maddie: Edge cases: orgs with multiple API keys — do we enforce per-org aggregates only, or per-key + per-org hybrid? We need both: per-key to isolate keys and per-org aggregate to prevent total overrun.
Jay: Hybrid enforcement is best: per-key throttle for noisy keys, per-org for budget. Keep config hierarchical.
Maddie: I'll spin up a short RFC with concrete numbers + rollout plan. Action items: Alex to prototype concurrency-first checks, Sam to design token-meter telemetry, Priya to draft fallback routing UX, Jay to propose default tiers.
Alex: On it. ETA end of week.
rate-limiter-bot: Deploy job queued: limiter-proto branch -> staging. ETA 20m :rocket:
Maddie: thanks, folks :thumbsup:
